extra_snippets: Georg (György) Lukács (1885–1971) was a literary theorist and philosopher who is widely viewed as one of the founders of “Western Marxism”. Lukács is best known for his pre-World War II writings in literary theory, aesthetic theory and Marxist philosophy.

Today, his most widely read works are the Theory of the Novel of 1916 and History and Class Consciousness of 1923. In History and Class Consciousness, Lukács laid out a wide-ranging critique of the phenomenon of “reification” in capitalism and formulated a vision of Marxism as a self-conscious transformation of society.

results.snippet: The Philosophical Leninism and Eastern 'Western Marxism' of Georg Lukács.Joseph Fracchia - 2013 - Historical Materialism 21 (1):69-93. A Review Of Young Lukács' Totality-dialectic.
extra_snippets: Not for the first time, certain stakes came to the boil again in the 1950s surrounding what became referred to as the ‘Lukács question’, namely the position of Georg Lukács under the shadow of Stalinism. What follows is an interview by Patrick Tort with Henri Lefebvre on the ‘Lukács question’, arising from an earlier lecture delivered by the latter in Hungary in 1955.

Most crucially, the interview touches on the concept of the ‘socialisation of society’, or dialectical totality, in which elements are incorporated as internally related to the structure of a whole. In contesting Stalinism as a discursive complex and for its defence of Lukács, the interview is a crucial material contribution to Marxist theory.

results.title: Steven M. Vogel, Nature and Natural Science in 'Traditional' and 'Critical' Marxism: Engels and Lukacs
results.snippet: Lukács on Science: A New Act in the Tragedy.Paul Burkett - 2013 - Historical Materialism 21 (3):3-15. A Review Of Young Lukács' Totality-dialectic.
extra_snippets: The status of nature and of the natural sciences in two distinct strains within Marxist philosophy is examined. "Traditional" or orthodox Marxism is represented by Engels: it is argued that his ...

He is forced to view dialectics as fundamentally non-epistemological, and as a result the significance of his own best insights--that the transformation of nature by labor is crucial to what nature is, that the "dialectics of nature" involves a dialectic between nature and society, that the end of "prehistory" involves the overthrow of the appearance of society as "like" nature --escapes him. ;The "critical" tradition is represented by Lukacs: here a much more appropriate and sophisticated epistemology is connected to a strong "separatist" thesis that society and nature must be kept sharply distinct by philosophy.

The model of knowledge as passive observation of an external and independent reality is epistemologically untenable, according to Lukacs, not because society is not such a realm, but because the model itself is inherently inconsistent, and issues in a series of fundamental antinomies.

Lukacs' separatism, however, seems to leave these antinomies in place , ignoring the radical and thorough-going character of his own epistemological critique. ;A non-separatist reading of Lukacs is attempted, in which it is suggested that the independence and externality of nature too, as well as that of society, must be put into question.

results.title: Baraneh Emadian, Lukács and Nietzsche: Revolution in a Tragic Key
results.snippet: Thus perceived, Lukács’s early corpus lends itself to a symptomatic reading. This essay seeks to extract the Nietzschean undercurrents of Lukács’s work through a reflection on the romantic anti-capitalist tendencies that the young Lukács shared with Nietzsche.
extra_snippets: György Lukács’s Marxist phase is usually associated with his passage from neo-Kantianism to Hegelianism. Nonetheless, Nietzschean influences have been covertly present in Lukács’s philosophical development, particularly in his uncompromising distaste for ...

For although it may appear that Nietzsche lacked a clear politics, his criticism of the bourgeois ethos as a structure based on debt/guilt [Schuld], and his critique of modern value-system and nihilism paved the way for the emergence of Lukács’s theory of reification.

The essay further traces the link between Lukács’s ‘romantic politics’ and the persistence of a thought of the tragic (a ‘tragic vision’) in his texts that, despite its temporary decline during his realist period, is undismissable in different constellations of his thought.

results.title: György Lukács, Conversations with Lukács
results.snippet: Spider and Fly: The Leninist Philosophy of Georg Lukács.Paul Le Blanc - 2013 - Historical Materialism 21 (2):47-75. A Review Of Young Lukács' Totality-dialectic.
extra_snippets: Using the technique of prepared questions, Conversations with Lukacs is a brilliant gathering of thoughts and insights covering topics as ontology, the techniques of manipulative societies, the pitfalls of combating Stalinism with Stalinist methods, and the problems of intellectuals in advanced capitalist societies.

Above all, there is the restatement of Lukacs unshaken conviction that the working class, with all the changes that have occurred in its way of life and composition, is still the historical carrier of social transformation. Lukacs's interlocutors in these four conversations are Hans Heinz Holz, Leo Kofler, and Wolfgang Abendroth.

Each of them engages Lukacs in separate dialogues, on being and consciousness (Holz), on society and the individual (Kofler), and on the elements of scientific politics (Abendroth). Lukacs, Abendroth, and Holz work toward a "Provisional Summary" in the last conversation.

This gives these conversations with Lukacs a more than anecdotal value; for the unmediated way in which thought is produced in conversation corresponds exactly to that primary level of experience, the data of everyday reality, whose theoretical value Lukacs emphasizes....
